notes.meaning: God speaks to Ezekiel again with a fresh message. Because people are often slow to realize their own wrongdoing and danger, God repeats his warnings many times.

The Lord tells Ezekiel a story about two sisters born to the same mother. These two sisters represent the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah, which originally began as one single family and nation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see this story as reflecting ancient patriarchal marriage laws, noting that the harsh imagery mirrors the real-life trauma of war and foreign conquest.

notes.meaning: Long ago while living in Egypt, both groups fell into idolatry, which means worshipping false gods instead of the true God. The prophet uses shocking, graphic pictures of sexual unfaithfulness to show how offensive this disloyalty was right from the beginning of their history.

The larger sister is named Oholah, representing the northern capital Samaria, and the younger sister is Oholibah, representing Jerusalem. Oholah means 'her own tent,' pointing to Samaria's man-made places of worship, while Oholibah means 'my tent is in her,' because God chose to put his holy temple in Jerusalem. Both belonged to God in a sacred covenant—a binding spiritual marriage—and bore him children.

Even though Samaria belonged to the Lord, she acted like an unfaithful wife. She chased after the powerful Assyrian empire, putting her confidence in their military strength and adopting their false gods.

Samaria was seduced by the outward splendor and pomp of Assyria's officers. They wore costly purple robes, rode fine horses, and looked handsome and capable, dazzling Israel into forgetting the true God.

Samaria gave herself completely to the leaders of Assyria and defiled herself with all their idols. By copying their corrupt ways and seeking their political favor, she held back nothing from her pagan allies.
Samaria also held on to the false worship she had first learned in Egypt. Her long-standing habit of chasing idols stayed with her, showing that her corrupt desires had never truly changed.
Because Samaria refused to trust him, the Lord handed her over to the very Assyrians she had courted. God in his justice turned the foreign power she relied on into the instrument that destroyed her.

The Assyrians stripped Samaria bare, dragged her people away into captivity, and struck down her citizens with the sword. Her terrible fall became a famous warning among the surrounding nations about the cost of turning away from God.

Jerusalem watched her sister Samaria get completely destroyed, but she failed to learn the lesson. Instead, she became even more depraved, running after foreign alliances and false gods with even greater passion.

Jerusalem also lusted after the Assyrians and their finely dressed military leaders. She admired their fine horses and handsome appearance rather than trusting the Lord who dwelled right in her midst.
The Lord saw that Jerusalem had become just as thoroughly corrupt as Samaria. Both sister kingdoms had chosen the exact same path of deserting God to trust in human armies.

Jerusalem went even further into sin when she saw carved figures and wall paintings of Babylonian warriors colored with bright red paint. Catching sight of Babylon's imperial grandeur stirred up an eager desire to seek their friendship.
These carvings portrayed Babylonian officers wearing wide military belts and large, flowing turbans. They looked so noble and powerful that Jerusalem became obsessed with getting close to them.
The moment Jerusalem saw these pictures, her longing took over and she sent messengers all the way to Chaldea. She actively invited a foreign pagan nation into a treaty instead of seeking God's help.

The Babylonians arrived and entered into an intimate alliance with Jerusalem, polluting her with their pagan practices. But after being defiled by them, Jerusalem grew weary and disgusted with her new masters and broke her loyalty.

Jerusalem openly showed off her faithlessness and shameless rebellion against both Babylon and God. In response, the Lord turned away from her in disgust, just as he had turned away from her sister Samaria.

Instead of repenting, Jerusalem multiplied her sins by thinking back fondly on her earliest days in Egypt. She decided to go back to the old idols and alliances that had tempted her when her nation was young.

Jerusalem longed for Egypt's powerful armies, using coarse animal descriptions to highlight Egypt's brute strength and energy. This harsh language is meant to make God's people sick of relying on pagan empires instead of the Lord.
Jerusalem eagerly went back to the shameful unfaithfulness of her past. She put her trust once again in the Egyptian leaders who had first drawn her into idolatry.

The Lord announces that he will stir up against Jerusalem the very lovers she had grown to despise. The Babylonians and their allies, whom she rejected and betrayed, will be brought against her from every direction.

A vast army made up of Babylonians, Chaldeans, various regional commanders, and Assyrian troops will advance on Jerusalem. The very warriors whose good looks and power Jerusalem once loved will now march to destroy her.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Latin commentators, following Jerome and the Vulgate Bible, understand Pekod, Shoa, and Koa not as regional tribes, but as titles of Babylonian rank and office, meaning rulers, nobles, and princes.

notes.meaning: This massive allied army will surround Jerusalem with chariots, heavy wagons, weapons, and shields. God will hand the city over to them so they can judge and punish her according to their own harsh and brutal laws.
